note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Definition of Share, Stock, and Kinds of Share Capital
explain: A share under Section 2(84) is a share in the share capital of a company and includes stock.
Share capital is divided into small measurable units called shares, each having a nominal face value.
Stock is a bundle of fully paid-up shares merged into one fund for convenience.
In Borland's Trustee v. Steel Brothers & Co Ltd, a share was held to be a shareholder's interest measured by a sum of money and rights/liabilities.
Section 43 classifies share capital of a company limited by shares into Equity Share Capital and Preference Share Capital.
Preference share capital carries preferential rights regarding dividend payment and repayment of capital during winding up.

flow.title: Conversion of Shares into Stock Process
steps: Issue initial shares to members
Ensure shares are fully paid-up
Obtain authorization under Articles
Pass resolution in General Meeting
Merge fully paid shares into stock
Reconvert stock to shares when needed

topics.example: Sun Bakers Limited has Rs. 50 lakh authorized capital divided into 5 lakh shares of Rs. 10 each. When allotted, holders become shareholders.
remember: Stock cannot be issued originally; only fully paid-up shares can be converted into stock under Section 61(1)(c).
Preference shares are presumed to be cumulative and non-participating unless stated otherwise (Scottish Insurance Corpn case).
mistakes: Confusing stock with partly paid-up shares; stock can only consist of fully paid-up shares.
Assuming a company can exist with only preference share capital; a company must have equity share capital.

quiz.q: Under Section 2(84) of the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following is correct regarding stock?
o: Stock can be issued directly to the public on incorporation
Stock includes partly paid-up equity shares
Stock is obtained by consolidating fully paid-up shares
Stock has a fixed nominal face value per unit
quiz.why: Stock is a collection or bundle of fully paid-up shares created after conversion, not issued originally.

quiz.q: If terms of issue are silent regarding participation rights of preference shares, what is the legal presumption?
o: They are participating in surplus assets
They are presumed to be non-participating
They automatically convert into equity shares
They carry equal voting rights with equity
quiz.why: As affirmed in Scottish Insurance Corpn Ltd, preference shares are presumed non-participating unless rights are expressly given.

topics.title: Equity Shares with Differential Rights
topics.section: Section 43(a) & Rule 4 of Companies (Share Capital & Debentures) Rules, 2014
explain: Equity shares can be plain vanilla (equal voting rights) or carry differential rights as to dividend, voting, or otherwise.
Issue must be authorized by Articles of Association and an Ordinary Resolution passed at a general meeting (postal ballot for listed companies).
Voting power of differential shares cannot exceed 74% of total voting power at any point of time.
Company must not have defaulted in filing annual accounts and returns for preceding 3 financial years.
Existing equity shares with normal voting rights cannot be converted into differential rights shares or vice versa (Rule 4(3)).

flow.title: Approval Process for Differential Rights Shares
steps: Check authorization in Articles
Ensure no default in financial filings
Verify voting power within 74% limit
Issue notice with Explanatory Statement
Pass Ordinary Resolution / Postal Ballot
Maintain details in Register of Members

topics.example: Company A issues Class B equity shares with 1 voting right for every 10 shares held, while Class A shares have 1 voting right per share.
remember: Maximum limit of voting power for DVR shares is 74% of total voting power.
Prohibition on conversion of normal equity shares into DVR shares and vice-versa is absolute.
mistakes: Thinking a Special Resolution is required for issuing DVR shares; an Ordinary Resolution is sufficient under Rule 4.
Believing companies can convert existing ordinary shares into shares with differential rights.

quiz.q: What is the maximum permissible limit of total voting power for equity shares with differential rights?
quiz.why: Rule 4(1)(c) mandates that total voting power of DVR shares shall not exceed 74% of total voting power at any point.

quiz.q: Can a company convert its existing equity shares with normal voting rights into equity shares with differential voting rights?
o: Yes, by passing a Special Resolution
No, Rule 4(3) strictly prohibits such conversion
quiz.why: Rule 4(3) prohibits the conversion of existing equity share capital with voting rights into differential rights and vice versa.

topics.title: Share Certificates and Duplicate Certificates
topics.section: Section 46 & Rules 5, 6, 7 of Companies (Share Capital & Debentures) Rules, 2014
explain: A share certificate issued under common seal or signed by 2 directors (or 1 director and Company Secretary) is prima facie evidence of title.
In depository form, records of the depository serve as prima facie evidence of beneficial ownership.
Renewed certificates are issued on surrender of defaced/mutilated certificates; fee capped at Rs. 50 per certificate.
Duplicate certificates for lost/destroyed shares are issued within 3 months for unlisted companies and 45 days for listed companies.
Register of Renewed and Duplicate Share Certificates must be maintained permanently in Form SH-2.
Issuing duplicate shares with intent to defraud attracts fine up to 10 times face value or Rs. 10 crore (whichever is higher) plus Section 447 action.

flow.title: Issuance of Duplicate Share Certificate
steps: Receive request for lost/destroyed certificate
Verify proof of loss and indemnity bond
Obtain Board consent
Print 'Duplicate issued in lieu of Share Cert No...'
Issue within 3 months (unlisted) / 45 days (listed)
Record details in Form SH-2 permanently

topics.example: Raj loses his physical share certificate. Upon submitting an affidavit and indemnity bond, the unlisted company issues a duplicate certificate in 60 days.
remember: Time limit for issuing duplicate shares: Unlisted = 3 months; Listed = 45 days.
Form SH-1 for Share Certificate; Form SH-2 for Duplicate Certificate Register.
mistakes: Believing share certificate is a negotiable instrument; it is only prima facie evidence of title.
Assuming duplicate share certificates can be issued without Board consent or proof of loss.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time limit for an unlisted company to issue a duplicate share certificate from submission of complete documents?
quiz.why: Rule 6 specifies that unlisted companies must issue duplicate share certificates within 3 months.

quiz.q: In which form must a company maintain the register of renewed and duplicate share certificates?
quiz.why: Particulars of renewed and duplicate share certificates must be entered in Form SH-2 and preserved permanently.

topics.title: Voting Rights of Shareholders
explain: Equity shareholders have a right to vote on every resolution placed before the company.
Voting right on a poll is proportional to the share in paid-up equity share capital (Nidhi company capped at 5% of total voting rights).
Preference shareholders can vote ONLY on resolutions affecting their rights, winding up, or reduction/repayment of capital.
If preference dividend is unpaid for 2 years or more, preference shareholders gain the right to vote on ALL resolutions.
Proportion of voting rights of equity to preference shareholders is based on their respective paid-up capital ratio.

flow.title: Determination of Preference Shareholder Voting Rights
steps: Check resolution topic (winding up/rights/capital reduction)
If yes, preference shareholders vote on poll
If no, check if preference dividend unpaid for 2+ years
If unpaid for 2+ years, voting right granted on all resolutions
Calculate vote proportion based on paid-up capital ratio

topics.example: Preference dividend of ABC Ltd is unpaid for 2023-24 and 2024-25. From 1st April 2026, preference shareholders can vote on all company resolutions.
remember: 2 years of unpaid dividend gives preference shareholders full voting rights on all resolutions.
Section 47 does not apply to Private Companies or Specified IFSC Public Companies if their AOA/MOA provides so.
mistakes: Thinking preference shareholders can vote on every resolution from the day of allotment.
Assuming unpaid dividend for 1 year gives full voting rights; it requires 2 years or more.

quiz.q: When do preference shareholders get the right to vote on all resolutions placed before the company?
o: When dividend is unpaid for 1 year
When dividend is unpaid for 2 years or more
When company makes a profit but delays payment
They can never vote on all resolutions
quiz.why: Second Proviso to Section 47(2) grants voting rights on all resolutions if dividend is unpaid for 2 years or more.

quiz.q: For a Nidhi company, what is the maximum voting power a member can exercise on a poll?
quiz.why: Section 47(1)(b) notification restricts any member of a Nidhi Company from exercising more than 5% of total voting rights on poll.

topics.title: Variation of Shareholders' Rights
explain: Rights of any class of shares can be varied if authorized by MOA/AOA or not prohibited by terms of issue.
Requires written consent of holders of at least 75% (3/4th) of issued shares of that class OR a Special Resolution at a separate class meeting.
If variation affects rights of another class, consent of 75% of that other class must also be obtained.
Dissenting shareholders holding at least 10% of issued shares of that class can apply to NCLT within 21 days to cancel variation.
Variation does not take effect until confirmed by NCLT, and NCLT order must be filed with RoC within 30 days.

flow.title: Variation of Class Rights & Challenge Process
steps: Check MOA/AOA for variation clause
Obtain 75% consent in writing or SR at class meeting
If dissenters hold >= 10% shares, they apply to NCLT within 21 days
NCLT hears parties and passes order
File NCLT order with RoC within 30 days

topics.example: A class has 105 holders; 100 holders own 0.5% each (total 50%) and 5 holders own 10% each (total 50%). Consent requires holders of 75% of shares, not 75% of people.
remember: 75% requirement is based on issued shares of that class, not number of shareholders.
Application to NCLT by dissenting shareholders requires holding at least 10% of issued shares within 21 days.
mistakes: Calculating 75% based on head-count of shareholders instead of proportion of issued shares.
Confusing 21 days limit for applying to NCLT with 30 days limit for filing NCLT order with RoC.

quiz.q: What minimum percentage of issued shares must dissenting shareholders hold to apply to NCLT against variation of rights?
quiz.why: Section 48(2) specifies that holders of at least 10% of issued shares of that class who did not consent may apply to NCLT.

quiz.q: Within how many days of NCLT order must the company file a copy of the order with the Registrar under Section 48?
quiz.why: Section 48(4) mandates filing a copy of the NCLT order with the Registrar within 30 days of the date of order.

topics.title: Calls on Shares, Calls-in-Advance & Dividend Rights
explain: Calls on shares must be made on a uniform basis for all shares falling under the same class (Section 49).
Section 50 allows a company, if authorized by AOA, to accept calls-in-advance (uncalled unpaid amount).
Calls paid in advance do NOT confer additional voting rights until the amount is formally called up.
Interest on calls-in-advance can be paid if permitted by AOA (e.g., Table F permits interest up to 12% p.a.).
Section 51 allows payment of dividend in proportion to the amount paid-up on each share if authorized by AOA.

flow.title: Handling Calls-in-Advance
steps: Check AOA authorization for calls-in-advance
Receive advance payment from member
Do NOT grant additional voting rights on advance
Pay interest as per AOA/General Meeting decision
Adjust advance against regular calls when made

topics.example: Reena pays Rs. 10 per share (Rs. 4 in advance). In general meeting, she gets voting rights for Rs. 6 called-up amount only, not for Rs. 4 advance.
remember: Calls-in-advance do NOT give extra voting rights.
Section 51 allows pro-rata dividend based on paid-up amount only if authorized by Articles.
mistakes: Thinking a shareholder who pays calls in advance gains extra voting power immediately.
Assuming calls can be made on selected members of the same class arbitrarily (Galloway v. Halle Concerts Society).

quiz.q: Does a member paying calls-in-advance under Section 50 get voting rights on such advance amount?
o: Yes, proportional to the advance paid
No, advance payment confers no extra voting rights until called up
Yes, up to 10% extra voting rights
quiz.why: Section 50 note confirms advance payment does not entitle the member to extra voting rights until called up.

quiz.q: Under Section 51, a company can pay dividend in proportion to paid-up capital only if:
o: Authorized by its Articles of Association
It is a listed public company
quiz.why: Section 51 permits pro-rata dividend payment only if so authorized by the Articles of Association.

topics.title: Issue of Shares at Premium and Discount
explain: Section 52: Shares issued above face value generate Securities Premium, transferred to Securities Premium Account.
Securities Premium Account can be used for: bonus shares, writing off preliminary/issue expenses, redemption premium, and buy-back.
For prescribed companies under Section 133 (AS compliant), uses are restricted to: bonus shares, writing off issue expenses, and buy-back.
Section 53: Issue of shares at a discount is strictly VOID, except for Sweat Equity Shares (Section 54) or debt conversion under restructuring/resolution plan (Section 2A).
Penalty for violating Section 53: Officer in default fined up to amount raised or Rs. 5 lakh (whichever is less); company must refund money with 12% p.a. interest.

flow.title: Permitted Utilization of Securities Premium (General Companies)
steps: Collect premium on share issue
Transfer to Securities Premium Account
Issue fully paid bonus shares
Write off preliminary expenses
Write off share/debenture issue expenses
Provide premium on redemption / Buy-back

topics.example: Share face value Rs. 10 issued at Rs. 14. Differential Rs. 4 per share is credited to Securities Premium Account.
remember: Section 53 makes share issue at discount void (except sweat equity and RBI debt conversion).
Company refunding money under Section 53 must pay 12% p.a. interest.
mistakes: Believing prescribed Section 133 companies can use Securities Premium to write off preliminary expenses or redemption premium; they CANNOT.
Thinking debentures cannot be issued at a discount; Section 53 restriction applies to SHARES, not debentures.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a permissible use of Securities Premium for Section 133 prescribed AS-compliant companies?
o: Issue of fully paid bonus shares
Writing off issue expenses of shares
quiz.why: Under Section 52(3), Section 133 prescribed companies cannot use Securities Premium to write off preliminary expenses.

quiz.q: What rate of interest must a company pay when refunding monies for illegally issuing shares at a discount under Section 53?
quiz.why: Section 53(3) requires the company to refund monies received with interest at 12% per annum.

topics.title: Issue of Sweat Equity Shares
topics.section: Section 54 & Rule 8 of Companies (Share Capital & Debentures) Rules, 2014
explain: Sweat equity shares are equity shares issued to directors or employees at a discount or for non-cash consideration for know-how/IPR/value additions.
Must be authorized by a Special Resolution specifying number of shares, market price, consideration, and eligible directors/employees.
Special Resolution validity for allotment is maximum 12 months.
Annual Limit: Higher of 15% of existing paid-up equity capital OR Rs. 5 crore.
Overall Ceiling: Maximum 25% of paid-up equity capital at any time (Startup companies limit is 50% for up to 10 years from incorporation).
Lock-in Period: 3 years from date of allotment (non-transferable). Shares rank pari-passu with other equity shares.

flow.title: Sweat Equity Shares Issuance Steps
steps: Ensure class of shares already issued
Valuation by Registered Valuer
Pass Special Resolution in GM
Allot shares within 12 months
Impose 3-year lock-in period
Record in Form SH-3 register

topics.example: Tech Corp issues Rs. 4 crore worth of sweat equity shares to key developer for software patent. Approved by SR, locked in for 3 years.
remember: Lock-in period for sweat equity shares is strictly 3 years.
Overall cap = 25% of paid-up equity capital (50% for Startups up to 10 years).
mistakes: Assuming a company must be in business for 1 year before issuing sweat equity; the 1-year requirement was omitted in 2018.
Confusing annual limit (higher of 15% or Rs. 5 crore) with cumulative cap (25%).

quiz.q: What is the lock-in period for sweat equity shares issued to directors or employees?
quiz.why: Rule 8(5) specifies that sweat equity shares are locked-in and non-transferable for 3 years from allotment.

quiz.q: What is the maximum cumulative cap on sweat equity shares for non-startup companies?
quiz.why: Rule 8(4) caps total sweat equity shares at 25% of paid-up equity capital at any time.

topics.title: Issue and Redemption of Preference Shares & CRR
topics.section: Section 55 & Rule 9 of Companies (Share Capital & Debentures) Rules, 2014
explain: No company limited by shares can issue irredeemable preference shares.

Maximum tenor of redeemable preference shares is 20 years. Exception: Infrastructure projects (Schedule VI) can issue up to 30 years, provided at least 10% is redeemed annually from 21st year onwards.
Issue requires authorization in Articles and a Special Resolution.
Redemption must be out of profits available for dividend OR fresh issue proceeds. Shares must be fully paid-up.
When redeemed out of profits, nominal amount must be transferred to Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) Account.
Unredeemed Preference Shares (Section 55(3)): Company unable to redeem can issue further preference shares with 3/4th consent in value and NCLT approval.

flow.title: Preference Share Redemption & CRR Creation
steps: Ensure shares are fully paid-up
Identify source: Profits or Fresh Issue
If out of profits, transfer nominal amount to CRR
Pay premium out of profits/Securities Premium
Cancel preference shares
Use CRR only for fully paid bonus shares

topics.example: Company redeems 20,000 preference shares of Rs. 100 each at Rs. 120 out of profits. Transfer Rs. 20,00,000 (nominal value) to CRR Account.
remember: Maximum tenor = 20 years (30 years for Infra with 10% annual redemption from 21st year).
CRR can ONLY be used to issue fully paid bonus shares under Section 55(4).
mistakes: Transferring total redemption amount (including premium) to CRR; only NOMINAL value is transferred.
Believing partly paid preference shares can be redeemed; shares MUST be fully paid-up.

quiz.q: For infrastructure projects under Schedule VI, what is the maximum tenor for redeemable preference shares?
quiz.why: First proviso to Section 55(2) allows up to 30 years for infrastructure projects, subject to 10% annual redemption from 21st year.

quiz.q: Under Section 55(4), Capital Redemption Reserve Account can be utilized ONLY for:
quiz.why: Section 55(4) explicitly limits CRR utilization to paying up unissued shares to be issued as fully paid bonus shares.

topics.title: Transfer & Transmission of Securities and Personation
explain: Proper instrument of transfer (Form SH-4) duly stamped, dated, and executed by transferor & transferee must be delivered to company within 60 days of execution.
For partly paid shares applied by transferor alone, company sends Form SH-5 to transferee; transferee must give no-objection within 2 weeks.
Time limit to deliver certificates: Subscribers = 2 months; Allotment of shares = 2 months; Transfer/Transmission = 1 month; Allotment of debentures = 6 months.
Transmission occurs by operation of law (death, insolvency, lunacy); does not require Form SH-4.
Section 56(5) allows legal representative of a deceased person to transfer shares even if not registered as holder.
Section 57: Deceitful personation of shareholder is punishable with imprisonment from 1 to 3 years AND fine from Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 5 lakh.

flow.title: Share Transfer Registration Process
steps: Execute Form SH-4 (transfer deed)
Stamp and date the instrument
Deliver deed + share cert to company within 60 days
Verify signatures and documents
Issue new certificate within 1 month
Update Register of Members

topics.example: Richa inherits shares on father's death. She can directly execute transfer deed to sell shares to Stesley under Section 56(5) without registering herself first.
remember: Transfer deed delivery window = 60 days from execution date.
Delivery of certificate on transfer/transmission = 1 month.
mistakes: Confusing transfer (voluntary contract needing SH-4) with transmission (operation of law needing death cert/probate).
Thinking forged transfer passes good title; forged transfer is void ab-initio.

quiz.q: Within how many days from execution must Form SH-4 transfer deed be delivered to the company?
quiz.why: Section 56(1) requires instrument of transfer to be delivered to the company within 60 days of execution.

quiz.q: What is the punishment for personation of a shareholder under Section 57?
o: Imprisonment 6 months to 1 year or fine Rs. 50,000
Imprisonment 1 to 3 years AND fine Rs. 1 lakh to 5 lakh
Fine up to Rs. 10 lakh only
quiz.why: Section 57 prescribes imprisonment from 1 to 3 years AND fine from Rs. 1 lakh to 5 lakh.

topics.title: Refusal of Registration and Appeal against Refusal
explain: Private Company: If refusing transfer/transmission, must send Notice of Refusal stating reasons to transferor and transferee within 30 days of receipt of deed.
Appeal by Transferee (Private Co): Within 30 days of receiving refusal notice OR within 60 days of delivery of deed (if no notice received).

Public Company: Securities are freely transferable. Refusal without sufficient cause allows transferee to appeal to NCLT within 60 days of refusal notice OR within 90 days of delivery of deed (if no notice received).
NCLT Order: Dismiss appeal OR direct registration within 10 days OR direct rectification & damages.
Contravention of NCLT order: Imprisonment 1 to 3 years AND fine Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 5 lakh.

flow.title: Appeal Timeline for Refusal of Transfer (Private vs Public)
steps: Deliver transfer deed to company
Company sends refusal notice within 30 days
Private Co: Appeal within 30 days (notice) / 60 days (no notice)
Public Co: Appeal within 60 days (notice) / 90 days (no notice)
NCLT passes order
Company complies within 10 days

topics.example: Private Co fails to respond to transfer deed sent on 25th Nov 2025. Transferee can appeal to NCLT within 60 days (by 24th Jan 2026).
remember: Private Co Appeal: 30 days (with notice) / 60 days (without notice).
Public Co Appeal: 60 days (with notice) / 90 days (without notice).
mistakes: Assuming notice of refusal should be sent only to transferee; Section 58(1) requires notice to BOTH transferor and transferee.
Confusing appeal timelines between private companies and public companies.

quiz.q: If a private company does NOT send a notice of refusal, within what time limit can the transferee appeal to NCLT?
quiz.why: Section 58(3)(b) permits appeal within 60 days of delivery of instrument of transfer if no notice is sent by private company.

quiz.q: If a public company refuses transfer without notice, what is the appeal window for the transferee to apply to NCLT?
quiz.why: Section 58(4)(b) allows appeal within 90 days of delivery of instrument of transfer when no intimation is received from public company.

topics.title: Rectification of Register of Members
explain: An aggrieved person, member, or company may appeal to NCLT (or competent foreign court for foreign members) for rectification of Register of Members.
Grounds for appeal: Name entered without sufficient cause, name omitted without sufficient cause, or default/unnecessary delay in entering membership details.
Unnecessary delay is a question of fact (e.g., failure to register transfer within 1 month contrary to listing agreement).
NCLT can dismiss appeal OR direct transfer within 10 days OR direct rectification + damages.
Order of NCLT does not restrict the holder's right to transfer securities during pending proceedings unless suspended by NCLT.

flow.title: Rectification of Register Process
steps: Occurrence of wrong entry/omission/delay
Filing of appeal to NCLT by aggrieved person/member
NCLT hears parties
NCLT orders registration/rectification within 10 days
Company pays damages if ordered

topics.example: Company arbitrarily removes Mr. A's name from Register of Members. NCLT orders reinstatement of name within 10 days and awards litigation costs.
remember: Personal grievance is not necessary for locus standi; any shareholder can apply for proper register maintenance.
NCLT order for transfer execution must be completed within 10 days.
mistakes: Believing only the affected individual can apply for rectification; ANY member has locus standi under Section 59.
Assuming pending rectification completely blocks transfer of securities automatically.

quiz.q: Within how many days must a company register a transfer upon receiving an order from NCLT under Section 59(2)?
quiz.why: Section 59(2)(a) requires company to comply with NCLT order to register transfer/transmission within 10 days of receipt.

quiz.q: Under Section 59, who among the following can file an application for rectification of Register of Members?
o: Aggrieved person, any member, or the company
quiz.why: Section 59(1) grants right of appeal to an aggrieved person, any member of the company, or the company itself.

topics.title: Alteration of Share Capital & Notice to Registrar
explain: A limited company with share capital, if authorized by AOA, can alter capital clause in MOA by passing an Ordinary Resolution at General Meeting.

Ways of alteration (Section 61): Increase authorized capital, consolidate and divide shares into larger amounts, convert fully paid shares into stock (and vice versa), sub-divide shares into smaller amounts, or cancel un-taken shares.
Consolidation/division resulting in change in voting percentage requires NCLT approval.
Cancellation of un-taken shares under Section 61(1)(e) is NOT deemed to be reduction of share capital under Section 66.
Section 64: Notice of alteration, government conversion order, or redemption of preference shares must be filed in Form SH-7 with RoC within 30 days.
Penalty for default under Section 64: Company and officer in default fined Rs. 500 per day (max Rs. 5 lakh for company, Rs. 1 lakh for officer).

flow.title: Capital Alteration & Filing Workflow
steps: Check Articles of Association authorization
Pass Ordinary Resolution in GM
NCLT approval (if consolidation affects voting %)
Alter Memorandum of Association
File Form SH-7 with RoC within 30 days
RoC records altered MOA

topics.example: Share of Rs. 100 (Rs. 80 paid up) is split into 10 shares of Rs. 10 each (Rs. 8 paid up). Filed in Form SH-7 within 30 days.
remember: Cancellation of shares under Section 61 is NOT capital reduction under Section 66.
Form SH-7 must be filed with RoC within 30 days of capital alteration.
mistakes: Assuming Special Resolution is needed for Section 61 alteration; an Ordinary Resolution is sufficient.
Confusing share split/sub-division with capital reduction under Section 66.

quiz.q: What resolution is required in a general meeting to alter share capital under Section 61?
quiz.why: Section 61 requires an Ordinary Resolution passed at a general meeting, provided AOA authorizes it.

quiz.q: Within how many days must notice of capital alteration in Form SH-7 be filed with the Registrar under Section 64?
quiz.why: Section 64(1) mandates filing Form SH-7 with altered MOA within 30 days of alteration.

topics.title: Further Issue of Share Capital / Rights Issue
explain: When increasing subscribed capital, further shares must be offered first to existing equity shareholders in proportion to paid-up capital (Rights Issue).
Offer period: Notice must specify acceptance time - not less than 15 days (7 days under Rule 12A) and not exceeding 30 days.
Notice must be dispatched at least 3 days before opening of issue (Private company shorter notice allowed if 90% members consent).
Renunciation: Shareholders have right to renounce offer in favor of another person unless AOA restricts.
ESOP (Section 62(1)(b)): Offered to employees via Special Resolution (Ordinary Resolution for private/IFSC public companies with clean filing record).
Preferential Allotment (Section 62(1)(c)): Offered to any person for cash/non-cash if authorized by Special Resolution and valuation report of Registered Valuer.
Section 62 does NOT apply to conversion of debentures/loans into equity pursuant to prior Special Resolution approval or Government order (Sections 62(3)-(6)).

flow.title: Rights Issue Offer Process
steps: Prepare Letter of Offer specifying share count
Dispatch notice at least 3 days before opening
Offer open for 15-30 days (min 7 days under Rule 12A)
Members accept, renounce, or decline
Board disposes un-subscribed shares non-disadvantageously
Allot shares and file PAS-3 in 30 days

topics.example: Suzlon Energy offers 1:10 rights issue. Shareholders get 1 share for every 10 shares held, with right to renounce to others.
remember: Offer open period = 15 to 30 days (min 7 days per Rule 12A).
Notice dispatch = at least 3 days before issue opening.
mistakes: Calculating 90% consent for shorter notice in private companies based on shareholding instead of number of members.
Thinking government conversion under Section 62(4) requires shareholder approval.

quiz.q: What is the minimum notice dispatch requirement before the opening of a Rights Issue under Section 62(2)?
quiz.why: Section 62(2) states notice must be dispatched to all existing shareholders at least 3 days before issue opening.

quiz.q: For a private company to adopt a shorter notice period for rights issue, what consent threshold of members is required?
quiz.why: Proviso to Section 62(2) allows shorter notice in private companies if 90% of members give consent in writing/electronic mode.

topics.title: Issue of Bonus Shares
explain: Bonus shares are fully paid-up shares issued free of cost to existing members proportionately by capitalizing profits/reserves.
Permitted Sources (Section 63(1)): Free reserves, Securities Premium Account, Capital Redemption Reserve Account.
Prohibited Source: Bonus shares CANNOT be issued by capitalizing Revaluation Reserve.
Pre-requisites: Authorized by AOA, recommended by Board & authorized in GM, no default in debt/deposit payments or employee statutory dues, partly paid shares made fully paid-up.
Once Board recommends a bonus issue, it CANNOT subsequently withdraw it (Rule 14).
Bonus shares CANNOT be issued in lieu of dividend.

flow.title: Bonus Share Issuance Checklist
steps: Check AOA authorization
Verify reserve sources (Free Reserves, SPA, CRR)
Ensure no default in debt/deposit/statutory dues
Ensure outstanding partly paid shares are fully paid
Board recommendation & GM authorization
Allot bonus shares without right of withdrawal

topics.example: Company declares 1:2 bonus issue. Holder of 100 fully paid equity shares gets 50 additional fully paid shares free of cost.
remember: Revaluation Reserve can NEVER be used for bonus issue.
Board recommendation of bonus issue CANNOT be withdrawn under Rule 14.
mistakes: Issuing bonus shares to partly paid-up shares without first making them fully paid-up.
Believing bonus shares can be declared as a replacement for cash dividend.

quiz.q: Which of the following funds CANNOT be utilized for issuing bonus shares under Section 63(1)?
quiz.why: Proviso to Section 63(1) prohibits issuing bonus shares by capitalizing reserves created by revaluation of assets.

quiz.q: Can a company withdraw a bonus share issue after the Board has once announced its recommendation?
o: Yes, by passing an Ordinary Resolution
quiz.why: Rule 14 of Share Capital Rules states a company that announced Board recommendation for bonus issue cannot withdraw it.

topics.title: Reduction of Share Capital
explain: Company limited by shares/guarantee can reduce share capital by Special Resolution confirmed by NCLT.
Methods: Extinguish/reduce liability on un-paid capital, cancel lost/unrepresented paid-up capital, or pay off excess paid-up capital.
Tribunal gives notice to CG (Regional Director), RoC, SEBI (listed co), and creditors; representations must be made within 3 months.
If no representation within 3 months, it is presumed they have no objection.
NCLT confirms reduction if creditor debts are discharged/determined/secured/consented AND auditor certifies accounting treatment complies with Section 133.
Certified copy of NCLT order and approved minutes must be filed with RoC within 30 days.

flow.title: Capital Reduction Workflow
steps: Pass Special Resolution in GM
Apply to NCLT with Auditor Certificate
NCLT issues notice to CG, RoC, SEBI, Creditors
Wait 3 months for representations
NCLT confirms order upon creditor satisfaction
File NCLT order + minutes with RoC in 30 days

topics.example: Company calls Rs. 7 on Rs. 10 share, then decides not to call remaining Rs. 3 and reduces share face value to Rs. 7 fully paid.
remember: Representation period for CG/RoC/Creditors = 3 months from notice date.
Filing NCLT order with RoC = within 30 days of receipt.
mistakes: Confusing capital reduction under Section 66 with buy-back under Section 68 or share cancellation under Section 61.
Failing to obtain auditor's certificate regarding Section 133 AS compliance when applying to NCLT.

quiz.q: What is the timeline within which authorities/creditors must submit representations on capital reduction to NCLT?
quiz.why: Section 66(2) provides that Tribunal shall consider representations made within 3 months from receipt of notice.

quiz.q: Within how many days of receiving NCLT order must the company deliver certified copy of order and minutes to RoC under Section 66(5)?
quiz.why: Section 66(5) requires company to deliver certified copy of NCLT order and minutes to RoC within 30 days of receipt.

topics.title: Restrictions on Purchase of Shares or Financial Assistance
explain: No company limited by shares/guarantee can buy its own shares unless consequent reduction of capital is effected under Act (Section 67(1)).
Public company CANNOT give direct/indirect financial assistance (loans, guarantees, security) for purchase/subscription of its own shares or holding company shares (Section 67(2)).

Exceptions (Section 67(3)): Lending by banking company in ordinary course; provision of money for Employee Share Scheme (Rule 16 trust) up to 5% of paid-up capital + free reserves; loan to non-KMP/non-director employees up to 6 months' salary to buy fully paid shares.
Exemption: Section 67 does not apply to Private Companies meeting 3 conditions (no body corporate investment, borrowings < 2x capital or Rs. 50 crore, no default) and Nidhi companies.
Penalty: Company fined Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 25 lakh; Officer in default faces imprisonment up to 3 years AND fine Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 25 lakh.

flow.title: Financial Assistance Exemption Test under Section 67(3)
steps: Is assistance given by Banking Co in ordinary course?
OR is assistance for Trustee Employee Share Scheme (<= 5% limit)?
OR is loan to non-KMP employee (<= 6 months salary for fully paid shares)?
If any YES -> Assistance is PERMITTED
If all NO -> Assistance is PROHIBITED

topics.example: OLAF Ltd gives Rs. 2,40,000 loan (6 months' salary) to HR Manager (non-KMP) to buy fully paid shares. This is valid under Section 67(3)(c).
remember: Employee loan cap = 6 months' salary for fully paid shares.
Trust scheme cap = 5% of aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves.
mistakes: Giving loan to employees to buy PARTLY paid-up shares; loan is permitted ONLY for fully paid-up shares.
Extending employee loan exception to Directors or Key Managerial Personnel.

quiz.q: What is the maximum loan amount a company can extend to its non-KMP employee to buy fully paid shares under Section 67(3)(c)?
quiz.why: Section 67(3)(c) restricts loan to employees to an amount not exceeding 6 months' salary.

quiz.q: What aggregate value cap applies to shares purchased by trustees under Employee Share Schemes under Rule 16?
o: 2% of paid-up capital and free reserves
5% of paid-up capital and free reserves
10% of paid-up capital and free reserves
25% of paid-up capital and free reserves
quiz.why: Rule 16 Note 3 specifies that value of shares shall not exceed 5% of aggregate paid-up capital and free reserves.

topics.title: Buy-Back of Securities & Restrictions
explain: Sources of Buy-Back (Section 68(1)): Free reserves, Securities Premium Account, or Proceeds of fresh issue of different kind of shares/securities.

Limits & Approval: Board Resolution up to 10% of paid-up equity capital + free reserves; Special Resolution up to 25% of total paid-up capital + free reserves (equity buy-back capped at 25% of paid-up equity capital in a FY).
Debt-Equity Ratio post buy-back must not exceed 2:1.
Time Limits: Buy-back must be completed within 12 months of resolution. Gap between two buy-back offers must be at least 1 year.
Declaration of Solvency (Form SH-9): Filed with RoC/SEBI before buy-back, signed by 2 directors (including MD), for 12 months solvency.
Extinguishment: Destroy securities within 7 days of completion. Cooling Period: No fresh issue of same shares for 6 months (except bonus/conversions).
Section 69: Transfer nominal value of shares bought back from free reserves/SPA to Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR).

Section 70: Buy-back prohibited through subsidiary/investment co, or if default exists in deposits, debentures, preference shares, dividend, term loan, or filings (Sec 92, 123, 127, 129). 3-year lapse required post default remedy.

flow.title: Buy-Back Execution & Compliance Flow
steps: Check AOA authorization & 2:1 debt-equity ratio
Pass BR (<=10%) or SR (<=25%)
File Declaration of Solvency (SH-9) & Letter of Offer (SH-8)
Keep offer open for 15 to 30 days
Complete payment within 7 days of verification
Extinguish securities in 7 days & transfer nominal value to CRR
File Return of Buy-back (SH-11) within 30 days

topics.example: Company buys back 8% equity shares using free reserves. It transfers nominal face value of bought shares to CRR and destroys shares in 7 days.
remember: Board approval limit = 10% of paid-up equity + free reserves; SR limit = 25%.
Physical destruction of bought-back shares = within 7 days.
Cooling period for fresh issue of same class = 6 months.
mistakes: Making a buy-back offer within 1 year of the closure of the preceding buy-back offer.
Thinking buy-back can be done out of proceeds of fresh issue of the SAME kind of shares.

quiz.q: What is the maximum post-buyback ratio of debt (secured and unsecured) to paid-up capital and free reserves permitted under Section 68(2)(d)?
quiz.why: Section 68(2)(d) mandates that post buy-back debt to paid-up capital and free reserves ratio shall not be more than 2:1.

quiz.q: Within how many days of completion of buy-back must a company physically destroy the bought-back securities under Section 68(7)?
quiz.why: Section 68(7) mandates physical destruction of bought-back securities within 7 days of completion of buy-back.

topics.title: Debentures, Debenture Trustee & DRR
explain: Debenture (Section 2(30)) includes debenture stock, bonds, or debt instruments, secured or unsecured.
Debentures carrying voting rights are strictly PROHIBITED (Section 71(2)).
Tenor of Secured Debentures: Max 10 years (up to 30 years for Infrastructure projects/companies/NBFCs). Charge created on specified assets in favor of Debenture Trustee.
Debenture Trustee (Section 71(5)): Mandatory if prospectus/offer issued to > 500 persons. Written consent required; Trust Deed in Form SH-12 executed within 3 months of offer closure.

Disqualifications for Trustee: Shareholder with beneficial interest, promoter/director/employee of co/holding/subsidiary, relative of KMP/director, indebted person, guarantor, or person having pecuniary relationship >= 2% turnover/gross income or Rs. 50 lakh.
Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR): Created out of dividend-eligible profits. Unlisted companies (non-NBFC/HFC) must maintain DRR equal to 10% of outstanding debentures.
Investment Requirement: By 30th April each year, invest/deposit at least 15% of debentures maturing during the year ending 31st March of next year in specified unencumbered securities.

flow.title: Secured Debenture Issue & Trustee Compliance
steps: Pass SR if debentures convert to equity or borrow > capital+reserves
Appoint Debenture Trustee (mandatory if offer > 500 persons)
Obtain trustee written consent
Create charge on assets within 10 years (30 for Infra)
Execute Trust Deed in Form SH-12 within 3 months
Maintain 10% DRR & 15% annual investment by 30th April

topics.example: Company issues secured debentures to 600 members. It appoints an independent Debenture Trustee and executes Form SH-12 trust deed within 3 months.
remember: Debentures CANNOT carry voting rights under any circumstances.
Debenture Trustee required if subscribers > 500.
Trust deed Form SH-12 execution = within 3 months of offer closure.
Annual investment requirement = 15% of maturing debentures by 30th April.
mistakes: Appointing a shareholder holding beneficial interest as a debenture trustee.
Believing debenture holders acquire voting rights if interest is unpaid for 2 years (unpaid voting rights apply ONLY to preference shares).

quiz.q: Appointment of one or more Debenture Trustees is mandatory if a company offers debentures to more than how many persons?
quiz.why: Section 71(5) requires appointment of debenture trustees prior to issue if offer/invitation exceeds 500 persons.

quiz.q: By what date each year must a company invest or deposit at least 15% of its debentures maturing during the year ending 31st March of next year?
quiz.why: Rule 18(7)(c) mandates investing/depositing at least 15% of maturing debentures by 30th April of each year.
